newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestine International Bank opens in West Bank.
newsitem.headline: Palestine International Bank opens in West Bank.

text.p: The Palestine International Bank (PIB) opened for business on Saturday promising improved computerised banking services to Palestinians in the West Bank and overseas customers.

PIB, based in the West Bank town of El-Bireh, is the sixth Palestinian-owned bank in the West Bank and Gaza. There are 18 banks with 73 branches - mainly Jordanian and Egyptian - operating in the West Bank and Gaza, the Palestinian Finance Ministry said.
Issam Abu Issa, president of PIB's board of directors, said at the opening ceremony the bank would have a technological edge over its competitors.

"We have the only automated dealing room in Palestine, a self-service Web site, treasury services and we will be the first bank in the Middle East, not only in Palestine, to offer home banking 24 hours a day, seven days a week," Abu Issa told Reuters.

He said PIB was capitalised at $20 million dollars and 60 percent of its shareholders are Palestinian and Arab investors living abroad, including senior Qatari officials. The rest are local Palestinian businessmen.

"We are aiming to invest locally, unlike most other banks which transfer its deposits in banks abroad and invest a small part of it in Palestine," Abu Issa said. "Despite harsh economic conditions and the closures, we are determined to do that."
The Palestinian Authority has complained of a hesitation to lend money to the private sector for development projects.

Mohammed Shtayeh, director of the Palestinian Economic Council for Development and Reconstruction (PECDAR) accused banks in the West Bank and Gaza Strip of "sucking" assets and depositing them in headquarters abroad.

"Bank deposits are around $1.9 billion of which only 19 percent has been lent out. Of this 19 percent, eight percent was lent out to the Palestinian Authority which means that less than 10 percent was lent to the private sector and the rest goes outside the country," Shtayeh said.

"This is unacceptable and very serious, and a challenge that the Palestinian Monetary Authority has to address. It has to introduce explicit banking regulations to regulate the work of banks," he told Reuters.
He added that the Palestinian Authority had to provide a healthy investment environment to prevent capital flight and attract new investors.
The frequent sealing off of Palestinian areas by Israel in the wake of suicide bombings by Moslem militants has led to the deterioration of the already ailing Palestinian economy.
Political instability has scared off potential Arab investors and development projects depend on irregular and insufficient funds from international donors.
The Palestinian Monetary Authority, which functions as a central bank for the Palestinian Authority, said in January bank deposits in 1996 reached $1.722 billion.
The banking sector began to develop in self-ruled areas after the PLO's takeover of parts of the West Bank and Gaza under the 1993 PLO-Israeli peace deal.
